summary: This informational memo records requirements from 3GPP Release 5 for SIP. 3GPP chose SIP as the session setup protocol for the IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS), and some of its needs were not met by SIP at the time.

eli5.summary: A phone standards group chose SIP for its multimedia network and listed what it still needed from SIP. This document passes that wish list to the IETF.

questions: what is a sip outbound proxy
subtitle: The wish list that the 3GPP cellular standards group handed to the IETF when it chose SIP for its multimedia network.

tldr.problem: 3GPP picked the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) to set up multimedia sessions in its IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS), but SIP had never been checked against the needs of a cellular network, such as scarce radio bandwidth, roaming, charging and strong authentication.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes the Release 5 IMS and lists the requirements 3GPP has on SIP, grouped by topic, often with a note on which existing SIP mechanism might already satisfy each one.
tldr.outcome: It is advisory only. The IETF said it would not answer point by point: some requirements have been or will be met by SIP extensions, some by existing capabilities, and some may not be addressed at all.

today: RFC 4083 is an Informational memo published in May 2005, and the registry metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It records requirements for Release 5 only; the text itself says later 3GPP releases may add more.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
3GPP selected SIP to establish and tear down multimedia sessions in the IP Multimedia Subsystem (IMS). This memo defines the requirements that apply to using SIP in cellular networks, in particular in the 3GPP IMS for Release 5 of the 3GPP specifications. Later releases may add further requirements.

The document is advisory. Its main purpose is to help the IETF understand the IMS environment so it can evolve SIP more effectively. It states that the IETF will not respond point for point, and it does not specify any protocol, so the RFC 2119 key words do not apply to it.
sections.eli5: It is a letter that says: here is what we need from SIP for our phone network, please read it so you understand us. It does not order anyone to do anything.

sections.title: The 3GPP IMS in Brief
sections.content:
A subscriber belongs to a home network, where services are triggered and may be executed. The home network has a SIP serving proxy that also acts as a SIP registrar, and authentication and authorization servers. Users are authenticated in the home network. It may also have SIP edge proxies as first entry points, found through DNS NAPTR and SRV records.

A SIP outbound proxy supports the user agent. It is typically in the visited network, may be in the home network, keeps security associations with terminals and interworks with resource management in the packet network. It is assigned after the device connects to the access network and does not change while the device stays attached, so the mobile can move freely inside that access network.

Home and visited networks may also deploy a SIP hiding proxy to hide network configuration. Terminals first use GPRS to attach and get an IPv6 prefix, and these GPRS procedures must finish before any IP multimedia session can be established.
sections.eli5: Your phone first connects to the radio network, then talks to a nearby helper (the outbound proxy) which passes its messages on to your home company, where you are checked and your services live.

sections.title: General, Registration and Compression Requirements
sections.content:
The general requirements are guidelines: use the radio interface efficiently, keep session setup time minimal, ask for minimal support in the terminal, work the same for roaming and non-roaming, leave terminal mobility to the access network, and support IPv6, since the IMS is designed solely for IP version 6.

The device must learn the outbound proxy address through a general mechanism; the memo says the DHCPv6 option in RFC 3319 seems to fulfill it. A user must register before receiving any session invitations, and 3GPP mandates that the device registers before initiating a session. One registration must be enough to be reachable from both home and visited networks. The home network must learn the visited network identity at registration time to validate a roaming agreement. The memo suggests a REGISTER with an expiration timer of 0 for de-registration, and the SIP event notification and registration event package for network-initiated de-registration or re-registration.

Because the radio interface is scarce, there must be a way to compress SIP messages between the device and the outbound proxy. The solution must work with several compression algorithms, be extensible, minimize the effect on access networks, be optional to use and be able to recover from decompression errors.
sections.eli5: Radio airtime is like a narrow pipe, so messages must be small, the sign-in must happen once, and the system should work the same at home and abroad.

sections.title: Identities, Routing and Hiding
sections.content:
Each user has a private user identity, assigned by the home operator in the form of a Network Access Identifier, used for authentication, authorization, administration and possibly accounting. It is not used for routing and is not accessible to the end user. Users also have one or more public user identities, which are SIP URIs or E.164 numbers. Public identities are not authenticated by the IMS, but the network checks that they are associated with the registered private identity. It must be possible to register all identities in one user profile with a single request.

Routing inside the IMS must use SIP URLs, so E.164 numbers are translated; the memo suggests a database such as ENUM could do it. All mobile-originated session setups must pass the outbound proxy and the serving proxy in the home network, which implies a source-routing mechanism. An INVITE need not follow the path taken by the REGISTER.

Hiding is required as a feature but optional to switch on: operators need not reveal their internal network structure or node IP addresses (other than firewalls and border gateways). The Cell-ID may be needed by the home network, and should be removed before signaling leaves the originating home network. Caller identity presentation, privacy, blocking and anonymity are also required, and the memo points to RFC 3325 and RFC 3323.
sections.eli5: You have a secret membership number that only the company uses, and a public name like a phone number that people use to reach you. The company checks that the two belong together.

sections.title: Sessions, Charging and Policy
sections.content:
For session release, the network must be able to end a session without asking the device to send a BYE, for instance when a prepaid caller runs out of credit or the terminal leaves coverage. Otherwise stateful proxies can suffer memory leaks from hanging state machines. The memo suggests a transparent back-to-back user agent.

Charging supports both prepaid (online) and postpaid (offline) models. Charging data is correlated using IMS Charging Identifiers (ICID), assigned by the first IMS entity in the signaling path and passed along the session path. Inter Operator Identifiers (IOI) are shared between home networks.

Other requirements: QoS signaling must be independent of SIP, and resources should be allocated before the destination is alerted when an application asks for it. The network must prevent theft of service, control radio resource use, prevent malicious use such as skipping Record-Route proxies, and minimize denial of service risk. Session description negotiation must be able to end with a reduced set of codecs per media stream, local policy may prohibit certain codecs, and the serving proxy can reject media types a subscription does not allow. The network must also be able to start re-authentication at any time, using triggers such as charging thresholds or session duration.
sections.eli5: The phone company must be able to hang up a call itself if you run out of credit, and it must keep careful count of who used what so the right person gets the bill.

sections.title: Security Model and Domains
sections.content:
The scope of IMS security is SIP signaling between SIP entities; protecting end-to-end media is not considered in Release 5. Each operator is its own domain of trust and shares a long-term security association with its subscribers. User agents must authenticate to the home network before using IMS resources, during registration and re-registration, and 3GPP intends to reuse UMTS AKA. Protection is hop by hop in two zones: the access domain between the device and the visited network, and the network domain between networks or inside the home network. They need different mechanisms.

Access domain requirements include scale (a subscriber base of up to a billion users), few extra bandwidth needs and round-trips, security without requiring public key cryptography, and independence from the transport protocol. Authentication must be strong and mutual, with credentials never sent as plain text. Message protection needs integrity, confidentiality where possible, based on the initial authentication and symmetric keys, and must be compatible with compression. Security mechanism negotiation must resist a man-in-the-middle who tries to force weaker security. Network domain security needs authentication, key agreement, integrity, replay protection and confidentiality between proxies, mandatory at least between two operators, and the memo suggests IPsec as in RFC 2401.

The memo's own security considerations section simply points to these sections as the security requirements it presents.
sections.eli5: There are two kinds of locks: a light one between your phone and the nearest helper, and a stronger one between the big companies' machines. Each is chosen to fit what it protects.
